l: Developer tools for the 75% who build their own.
p: 75% of Nord Pool's customer base connects directly via API. They are quants, data scientists, and developers who build and maintain their own trading infrastructure. Phase Nexa gives them better tools to do it.

Every energy trading company in Europe has developers writing the same code: ENTSO-E API wrappers that break when the format changes. Bid generators that need rebuilding for 15-minute MTUs. Position trackers held together with spreadsheets and prayer.
The ISVs want to sell you a platform. We want to give you libraries.

c: pip install nexa-marketdata

p: The European power market data landscape is fragmented. Every exchange has its own API, its own data format, its own quirks. The community alternatives (entsoe-py, kipe/nordpool) are volunteer-maintained and frequently break when APIs change.
nexa-marketdata provides a single, well-tested client that handles:
Multiple exchanges through a consistent interface
Rate limiting so you do not get blocked by exchange APIs
Caching to avoid redundant API calls
Type-safe models with Pydantic v2 and strict mypy compliance
No floats for money — all prices and volumes use Decimal
Set API credentials as environment variables before running:

c:
from nexa_marketdata import NexaClient
from nexa_marketdata.types import BiddingZone
import datetime

client = NexaClient()

# Day-ahead prices for NO2 (Southern Norway)
prices = client.day_ahead_prices(
    zone=BiddingZone.NO2,
    start=datetime.date(2025, 1, 1),
    end=datetime.date(2025, 1, 7),
)

print(prices.head())

export NORDPOOL_USERNAME="your-username"
export NORDPOOL_PASSWORD="your-password"
export ENTSOE_API_KEY="your-key-here"

c: pip install nexa-bidkit

p: Building bids for European power auctions is complex. The EUPHEMIA algorithm supports simple hourly orders, block bids, linked orders, and exclusive groups, each with specific constraints. Getting the domain model wrong means rejected bids or, worse, unintended market exposure.
Type-safe bid construction with Pydantic v2 and strict validation
DataFrame-first API — build curves directly from pandas DataFrames
15-minute MTU support across all bid types (EU transition: 30 Sept 2025)
EUPHEMIA compatibility — output formats compatible with European power market coupling
Comprehensive validation — EUPHEMIA compliance checks, data quality rules, temporal constraints
Nord Pool serialisation — converts your bids to Nord Pool Auction API payloads

l: Build a supply curve from a DataFrame

c:
import pandas as pd
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from nexa_bidkit import CurveType, MTUDuration, MTUInterval, from_dataframe

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "price": [10.5, 25.0, 45.0, 80.0],
    "volume": [50, 100, 75, 25],
})

mtu = MTUInterval.from_start(
    datetime(2026, 4, 1, 13, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/Oslo")),
    MTUDuration.QUARTER_HOURLY,
)

curve = from_dataframe(df, curve_type=CurveType.SUPPLY, mtu=mtu)

print(f"Total volume: {curve.total_volume} MW")
print(f"Price range: {curve.min_price} – {curve.max_price} EUR/MWh")

from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from nexa_bidkit import (
    BiddingZone, Direction, DeliveryPeriod, MTUDuration,
    block_bid, indivisible_block_bid, linked_block_bid, exclusive_group,
)

delivery = DeliveryPeriod(
    start=datetime(2026, 4, 1, 10, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/Oslo")),
    end=datetime(2026, 4, 1, 14, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/Oslo")),
    duration=MTUDuration.QUARTER_HOURLY,
)

# Partially fillable block bid (accepts 50%+ fill)
peak_bid = block_bid(
    bidding_zone=BiddingZone.NO1,
    direction=Direction.SELL,
    delivery_period=delivery,
    price=Decimal("55.0"),
    volume=Decimal("100"),
    min_acceptance_ratio=Decimal("0.5"),
)

# All-or-nothing block bid
must_run = indivisible_block_bid(
    bidding_zone=BiddingZone.NO1,
    direction=Direction.SELL,
    delivery_period=delivery,
    price=Decimal("25.0"),
    volume=Decimal("50"),
)

# Child bid: only accepted if parent accepted
ramp_up = linked_block_bid(
    parent_bid_id=must_run.bid_id,
    bidding_zone=BiddingZone.NO1,
    direction=Direction.SELL,
    delivery_period=delivery,
    price=Decimal("35.0"),
    volume=Decimal("25"),
)

Data quality: minimum volumes (0.1 MW), monotonic price steps
Temporal: gate closure deadlines, delivery periods within auction day

Payloads use camelCase aliases and serialise with .model_dump(by_alias=True) for direct use with the Nord Pool API.

from nexa_bidkit.nordpool import order_book_to_nord_pool

# Resolve Nord Pool contract IDs from their products API
def resolve_contract(mtu, zone):
    return f"{zone.value}-{mtu.start.hour}"

submission = order_book_to_nord_pool(
    book,
    auction_id="DA-2026-04-01",
    portfolio="my-portfolio",
    contract_id_resolver=resolve_contract,
)

print(f"Curve orders:        {len(submission.curve_orders)}")
print(f"Block orders:        {len(submission.block_orders)}")
print(f"Linked block orders: {len(submission.linked_block_orders)}")

Build, validate, and serialise mFRR energy activation market bids for the Nordic TSOs.
Python library for building, validating, and serialising mFRR energy activation market (EAM) bids for the Nordic TSOs: Statnett (NO), Energinet (DK), Svenska kraftnät (SE), and Fingrid (FI).
This library is under active development. The API, documentation, and feature set are subject to change before the stable release.

c: pip install nexa-mfrr-nordic-eam
pip install nexa-mfrr-nordic-eam[pandas]

p: The Nordic mFRR energy activation market (EAM) went live on 4 March 2025 as part of the Nordic Balancing Model (NBM). BSPs submit bids via ECP/EDX as CIM XML documents to their connecting TSO.
This library handles the full BSP document workflow:
Build simple bids — divisible and indivisible bids with full attribute support (volume, price, resource, product type, duration constraints)
Technically linked bids — prevent double-activation across consecutive MTUs
Conditionally linked bids — adjust availability based on prior-MTU activation outcome
Complex bid groups — ExclusiveGroup, MultipartGroup, InclusiveGroup with group-level validation
TSO configuration — Statnett (NO), Energinet (DK), Svenska kraftnät (SE) fully configured; Fingrid planned
Validate before you send — common and TSO-specific rules, pre-MARI and post-MARI price limits
Serialise to CIM XML — generates compliant ReserveBid_MarketDocument XML per the NBM ReserveBid schema
Timing helpers — gate closure calculations, MTU boundaries, DST handling, MARI vs pre-MARI timing
This library generates and will eventually parse the XML documents you send and receive over ECP. It does not manage your ECP/EDX endpoint — that infrastructure is deployed and operated separately.

l: Submit a simple bid to Statnett

c:
from nexa_mfrr_eam import (
    Bid, BidDocument, MarketProductType,
    BiddingZone, TSO, MARIMode,
)

# Divisible up-regulation bid: 50 MW at 85.50 EUR/MWh
bid = (
    Bid.up(volume_mw=50, price_eur=85.50)
    .divisible(min_volume_mw=10)
    .for_mtu("2026-03-21T10:00Z")
    .resource("NOKG90901", coding_scheme="NNO")
    .product_type(MarketProductType.SCHEDULED_AND_DIRECT)
    .build()
)

# Wrap in a document targeting Statnett
doc = (
    BidDocument(tso=TSO.STATNETT)
    .sender(party_id="9999909919920", coding_scheme="A10")
    .add_bid(bid)
    .build()
)

# Validate against Statnett rules
errors = doc.validate(mari_mode=MARIMode.PRE_MARI)
if not errors:
    xml_bytes = doc.to_xml()
    # Send xml_bytes via your ECP endpoint

p: Multipart bids offer volume at multiple price levels for the same MTU. If a higher-priced component is accepted, all cheaper components must also be accepted.

c:
from nexa_mfrr_eam import Direction, MultipartGroup, BiddingZone, TSO, BidDocument

group = (
    MultipartGroup(bidding_zone=BiddingZone.NO2)
    .direction(Direction.UP)
    .for_mtu("2026-03-21T10:00Z")
    .resource("NOKG90901", coding_scheme="NNO")
    .add_component(volume_mw=20, price_eur=50.00)
    .add_component(volume_mw=15, price_eur=75.00)
    .add_component(volume_mw=10, price_eur=120.00)
    .build()
)

doc = (
    BidDocument(tso=TSO.STATNETT)
    .sender(party_id="9999909919920", coding_scheme="A10")
    .add_bids(group)
    .build()
)

p: Technical links prevent double-activation when a resource spans consecutive MTUs.

c:
from nexa_mfrr_eam import Bid, TechnicalLink, BiddingZone, TSO, BidDocument

link = TechnicalLink()

bid_qh1 = (
    Bid.up(volume_mw=30, price_eur=60.00)
    .for_mtu("2026-03-21T10:00Z")
    .resource("NOKG90901", coding_scheme="NNO")
    .link(link)
    .build()
)

bid_qh2 = (
    Bid.up(volume_mw=30, price_eur=60.00)
    .for_mtu("2026-03-21T10:15Z")
    .resource("NOKG90901", coding_scheme="NNO")
    .link(link)
    .build()
)

doc = (
    BidDocument(tso=TSO.STATNETT)
    .sender(party_id="9999909919920", coding_scheme="A10")
    .add_bids([bid_qh1, bid_qh2])
    .build()
)

MCP server exposing Phase Nexa tools to LLM clients.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes Phase Nexa data and tools to LLM clients. Query market data, generate bids, and explore trading positions from Claude, ChatGPT, or any MCP-compatible client.

Trading desks are not just developers. Analysts, portfolio managers, and traders need access to the same data and tools without writing Python scripts. nexa-mcp bridges that gap by making Phase Nexa capabilities available through natural language.

Ask your LLM: "What were the day-ahead prices for NO1 yesterday?" or "Build me a block bid for 50 MW between 08:00 and 16:00 at 48 EUR/MWh" and get real answers backed by real data and real bid generation logic.
nexa-mcp implements the Model Context Protocol standard, exposing Phase Nexa libraries as tools that LLM clients can call.

Every Phase Nexa repository welcomes contributions. Each repo has a CONTRIBUTING.md with specific guidelines, but the general process is:
Create a feature branch from main
We use trunk-based development with squash merges. All PRs require CI to pass.
Bug reports: Found a bug? Open an issue on the relevant repo. Include your Python/Go version, exchange, and a minimal reproduction.
Feature requests: Open an issue describing what you need and why. Real-world use cases are the most persuasive.
Documentation: Typos, unclear explanations, missing examples. These are always welcome.
Exchange coverage: Adding support for a new exchange or data source? Open an issue first so we can discuss the approach.
Python repos: Ruff for linting and formatting, mypy for type checking, pytest for tests. See each repo's Makefile.
Go repos: Standard go fmt, go vet, golangci-lint. Follow HashiCorp-style patterns (clean interfaces, minimal dependencies, good error handling).
Issues: The best place for bug reports, feature requests, and technical discussion
